Build Your Own Budget Before the Sub Quotes Arrive

A trade-by-trade method for building your own GC budget before the sub quotes land, so bid leveling catches scope gaps in subcontractor quotes.

Jimmy Chavez
Founder and CEO, ConstructWise
Nov 6, 2026 8 min read

The low sub quote became your budget. Was it right? When the quotes land in a pile, the low one goes in the budget column and the team moves on to the next trade. What that trade should have cost before the quotes showed up never gets written down.

Why does the low sub quote become your budget?

Because it is the only number in the room. The drawings are out, the subs are pricing, and the estimator who has to carry a number for every trade has nothing of his own to hold a quote against.

So the lowest quote becomes the reference. The next quote is judged as high against it, and the buyout conversation starts from the sub's number instead of yours.

I read this as a process problem, not a software problem. The baseline never gets built, because bid week has no room for it. And a GC with no budget of his own, trying to buy out a job against three numbers that all came from somebody else, is a recipe for trouble. Let me show you what that trouble looks like.

The low quote that turned out to be the expensive one

On a $14 million medical office building, the low drywall quote came in at $1,042,000 and closed at $1,271,600, which is $3,600 more than the high quote we had set aside. Here is how a number you pick as the cheapest becomes the most expensive one on the job.

This one is a composite, with the names off and the numbers rounded, because the real versions belong to people who still bid against each other. Most estimators will recognize their own version by the second line.

Three quotes came in for the framing, drywall, and insulation package. The low was $1,042,000. The middle was $1,195,000. The high was $1,268,000, from the sub who had done our last three jobs and never once surprised us. The low number went into the budget. We had nothing of our own to level it against, only the low quote and a column of exclusions on page three that nobody read until the second week of framing.

The low number left out more than it carried. Firestopping at the rated penetrations was by others. The lobby was priced at a level 4 finish where the spec called for level 5. The shaft walls were carried as standard studs instead of shaft liner. Blocking for casework and grab bars was gone in one sentence. Every one of those came back as a change order, 27 of them over eight months, $184,000 in all.

Then the schedule slid four weeks when his crew thinned out for a bigger job across the county, and our general conditions at $11,400 a week ate another $45,600. Add it up. $1,042,000 at award, plus $184,000 in change orders, plus $45,600 in general conditions, and the package closed at $1,271,600. That is $3,600 over the quote we had called too high, before a single cost that never reaches a cost report.

What our own baseline would have caught

Had we built a budget of our own for that package before bid day, with every item in the package listed beside the number, the exclusions would have shown up on the first read instead of in the second week of framing. Our own takeoff would have carried the shaft liner, the level 5 lobby, the firestopping, and the blocking, because they are in the drawings and we would have priced them from what they cost us last time. The low quote would have read as short by roughly $184,000, which is almost exactly what it turned out to be.

And we had the sub history. The low sub had closed 14 percent over award on one of the prior jobs and 19 percent over on the other. The high sub had closed within one percent of award on all three of theirs, and on one of them sent us a $6,000 credit when a wall came out of the drawings. All of it was sitting in closed job files. Nobody had ever put it beside a quote on bid day.

Leveled against our own budget, with the package list and the closeout history on the same screen, those three quotes would have read differently. The low one was short. The middle one was in range with no track record. The high one was the only number on the table that was going to be the number at the end.

The most expensive quote was the most comprehensive one, and by closeout it was the most affordable one, too.

How it goes today
  • The low quote quietly becomes the budget
  • No in-house check on scope, price, or how that sub closed last time
  • Buyout starts from the sub's number, not yours
What changes
  • Build your own budget first, package by package, item by item
  • Drawings in, takeoff and prices out, from your Data Hub history, general conditions included
  • Conflicts between drawings and specs flagged before a sub sees them
  • Every quote leveled line by line, then refined through buyout with your margin held
What you get back

You award on scope, price, and track record. Not on the lowest number in the pile.

How do you build your own GC budget before the sub quotes arrive?

I would do it in the days before bid day, while the subs are still pricing. It takes one line per item of work and six habits.

  1. Split the job the way you will buy it. One trade package per scope you are sending out, in your own cost codes or in CSI MasterFormat if that is how you code. Match the packages you sent out, so every quote has a package to be held against.
  2. Break each package into its items of work. A package is not one line. Site work is asphalt paving, site concrete, landscaping, and fine grading, and asphalt paving is the Type B section, the overlay, the fabric interlayer, and the base. Every one of those gets its own line, with the quantity, the unit, and the spec section beside it. The line is where the apples to apples comparison happens, because a sub cannot leave an item out of a lump sum you never broke apart. On the medical job, shaft liner, level 5 at the lobby, firestopping, blocking, and lift access would each have been a line of their own, and the low quote would have shown a blank on all five.
  3. Take quantities from your own takeoff. Use the quantity you would hand a sub, not a lump sum. If a quantity is soft, say so on the line.
  4. Price each item from your own jobs. Pull what the same item cost you on the last jobs that look like this one, and favor what you paid at closeout over what you awarded. Adjust for size, location, and date, and write down what you adjusted.
  5. Give each package a band. A low bound you would be glad to buy the package at, and a high bound where you start asking questions. The real number lives somewhere between them, and the lines underneath tell you which item is pushing it one way or the other.
  6. Lock it before you open the first quote. Save it, date it, and do not edit that version after the quotes land. Once you have seen the low number, you will price toward it without meaning to. Refinements go on new dated lines beside the original as buyout teaches you things.

This is the work bid week never leaves room for, and it is what ConstructWise was built to do. Attach the drawings in the AI chat and ask for a scope package. The AI estimating software runs the quantity takeoff, splits the job into trade packages and items of work, and prices each one from your own history, general requirements and general conditions included. That is your baseline, built before a sub has seen the job.

From there it goes to work. It reads the drawings against the specs and the basis of design and flags where they fight. It surfaces the scope gaps, the items your package is missing and the items in a quote that are not in your scope, and drafts the RFI when a gap needs the architect. And when the quotes land, whether for MEP, sitework, or framing, it runs the bid leveling, lining every one up against your budget line by line, with the lumps spread and the exclusions carried.

Then comes the judgment no spreadsheet makes for you. You decide how much contingency to carry, how much markup to add, and where to set allowances while the drawings are still soft. You commit a number above the sub's proposal, hold at least a 5% margin, and still price it tight enough to win. ConstructWise runs that math with you, and that detailed number crunching is what we do best.

Watch out

A thin history gives a generic number. If you have never bought a trade like this one, your baseline for it is a starting point. Mark that line soft, and read its comparison with more caution than the others.

How do you tell a low quote from a short one?

You level the quotes inside each trade package, line by line against your items of work, and you pull up how each sub closed the last time you used him. The scope gaps between the subs show up as blanks, exclusions, and lumps that do not break apart. Where the package total lands against your band tells you which question to ask first.

Where the quote landsWhat to suspect firstWhat you do
Inside your bandThe scope probably matches yoursStill read the exclusions page against your item list for the package
One quote above your band, others insideScope you did not price, or a sub carrying riskAsk what is in the number that is not on your list. It may be the only complete quote in the pile
One quote below your band, others insideSomething left outFind the exclusion before you award, and price it back in
Every quote for the trade on the same side of your bandYour quantity or your unit priceRecheck your takeoff and your history for that package first
Inside your band, but the sub closed 10 percent or more over award last timeThe quote is the opening bid, not the priceCarry the quote at the sub's history, then compare it to the others

The fourth row matters. A baseline built from your own takeoff also audits your takeoff. When the subs agree with each other and disagree with you, check your quantity and your unit price before you question the subs.

The second and last rows are the ones the medical job taught me. The quote above your band may be the one that priced everything on your list, and a quote inside your band from a sub who never closes inside his own number is not inside your band. It is a down payment.

What do you do when your number and the quote disagree?

Treat the gap as a list of questions about the specific items where your package list and the quote part ways.

Call the sub and ask about those items. Keep your own number to yourself. If the sub has a good answer, write the revised number on a new dated line beside the original and note why. That is how the budget gets refined through the buyout process, one conversation at a time. The locked version stays as it was, so you can see later what you knew before the quotes landed.

This is the heart of it. The band starts wide, and every quote, every RFI, and every closeout pulls the low bound and the high bound closer together, until they bracket the number the job will actually cost. That narrowing is construction estimating in a nutshell. It does not stop when you award. It stops when the last check clears.

Then close the loop at job closeout. Once the final cost of the trade is known, write it down against the band you set, and write down who the sub was. That entry is the history your next baseline prices from, and it is the only thing that will tell you, two years from now, that the high quote was the cheap one.

Take this to your next bid

Six checks before the first quote gets opened

  • Every trade package matches the split you sent out.
  • Every package is broken into its items of work, one line each, checked against the drawings and specs.
  • Every line has a quantity from your takeoff, with soft ones marked.
  • Every line has a band built from your own recent jobs, priced at closeout.
  • Every sub you are about to open has his last closeout pulled up beside his quote.
  • The sheet is saved and dated before any quote is read.

Questions estimators ask

How do I know if a sub quote is missing scope?

Level it line by line against the items of work in that trade package. Anything on your lines that the quote does not mention, excludes by name, or buries in a lump it will not break apart is a gap to price back in before you compare it to the other quotes.

What is bid leveling in construction?

Bid leveling is comparing subcontractor quotes for the same trade package against each other and against your own budget, line by line, so a low number and a complete number can be told apart. You level on scope, not just price, and you pull up how that sub closed on past jobs before you award.

What are scope gaps in subcontractor bids?

Scope gaps are the items that fall between two trades or hide in a spec section, so no sub prices them and nobody notices until the field does. You catch them by leveling every quote against a written item list for the package, where a gap shows up as a blank, an exclusion, or a lump that will not break apart.

What is a baseline budget for a general contractor?

It is the construction cost estimating you do before the subs weigh in. It is your own independent price for each trade package, built from the plans and your takeoff and priced from your own history, before any sub quote arrives. You use it to judge quotes instead of letting the lowest quote set the budget, and you refine it as buyout goes on.

Should I build my budget before or after I get sub quotes?

Before, and lock it before you read the first quote. A budget built after you have seen the low number drifts toward it.

Should I ever award the highest quote?

Yes. The most expensive quote is often the most comprehensive one, and from a sub who holds his number it can be the most affordable one by the time you close out the job. A price that does not move is worth more than a price that starts low, and your own closeout records will show you which subs hold their price.
